# CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO

Yang Li Affiliation:  School of Software and Microelectronics, Peking
University, Beijing    Gongle Xue Affiliation:  School of Artificial
Intelligence, Peking University, Beijing    Yijia Guo Affiliation: 
School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing    Yuheng Yuan
Affiliation:  School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing   
Liwen Hu Affiliation:  School of Computer Science, Peking University,
Beijing    Lei Ma Affiliation:  School of Future Technology, Peking
University, Beijingly0376@stu.pku.edu.cn  lei.ma@pku.edu.cn^(†)
Corresponding author.

###### Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), especially Group
Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has been widely used to improve
reasoning in large language models. However, outcome-level rewards
provide only sparse supervision, and group-relative advantages vanish
when all sampled trajectories for a prompt are either correct or
incorrect. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) offers dense token-level
guidance, but its token preferences are not necessarily aligned with
trajectory correctness; empirical diagnostics show that OPSD signals
behave differently on correct and incorrect rollouts, with
teacher-positive and teacher-negative gap signals exhibiting different
noise profiles. These diagnostics are conducted under an OPSD-style
privileged teacher context for analysis only, whereas CAST training uses
answer-free self-teacher scoring.

Motivated by these observations, this work proposes CAST (Non-Privileged
Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO), an
answer-free self-distillation method for GRPO-style RLVR. CAST keeps the
verifier-grounded GRPO objective, but uses a stop-gradient self-teacher
to shape token-level advantages according to trajectory correctness.
Unlike prior self-distilled RLVR methods, CAST does not require
reference-solution-conditioned teacher scoring, keeps the self-teacher
log-probability gap active throughout training, and applies
bidirectional local advantage sign reversal: teacher-negative tokens in
correct trajectories can receive negative token-level advantages, while
teacher-positive tokens in incorrect trajectories can receive bounded
positive local advantages. For zero-variance all-correct and all-wrong
groups, CAST assigns bounded sign-constrained base advantages, so these
otherwise zero-gradient groups can contribute verifier-signed token
feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning show that CAST improves
RLVR training while retaining a lightweight, verifier-grounded
trajectory-level objective.

## 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a
widely used paradigm for improving reasoning in large language
models \[[4](#bib.bib8), [28](#bib.bib7), [22](#bib.bib9),
[7](#bib.bib12), [21](#bib.bib15)\]. Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO) \[[20](#bib.bib1)\] samples multiple trajectories per prompt and
estimates group-relative advantages from verifier outcomes, offering a
scalable alternative to critic-based policy
optimization \[[24](#bib.bib25), [3](#bib.bib21), [8](#bib.bib22)\].

Despite its success, GRPO provides only sparse, outcome-level
supervision \[[15](#bib.bib23), [30](#bib.bib3), [29](#bib.bib5),
[10](#bib.bib13)\]: it says little about which tokens help or hurt, and
the group-relative advantage vanishes when all rollouts for a prompt are
correct or all are incorrect \[[30](#bib.bib3), [13](#bib.bib14)\].
These zero-variance groups still contain useful consolidation or failure
signals, motivating dense token-level guidance that remains
verifier-grounded.

On-policy self-distillation \[[17](#bib.bib10), [1](#bib.bib11),
[32](#bib.bib4), [31](#bib.bib26), [6](#bib.bib27)\] supplies such
guidance, and recent RLVR variants \[[29](#bib.bib5), [12](#bib.bib17)\]
already exploit teacher–student gaps beyond sparse rewards. However,
three issues remain: gaps are not interpreted differently on correct
versus incorrect trajectories, teacher scoring often uses
answer-privileged contexts, and all-correct/all-wrong groups are
typically underused once group-relative advantages
collapse \[[11](#bib.bib2)\].
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Motivation: Correctness-Aware Self-Teacher Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
studies gap structure under an OPSD-style privileged diagnostic; CAST
training uses answer-free self-teacher scoring only.

We propose CAST (Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with
Advantage Flipping for GRPO). CAST keeps the verifier-grounded GRPO
objective, shapes token advantages with detached rollout/reference
teacher–student gaps, applies bidirectional local sign reversal, and
assigns bounded base advantages to zero-variance groups.

The contributions are:

- •
  Teacher–student gaps are analyzed under mathematical RLVR, showing
  different behavior across correctness and gap sign
  (Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Motivation: Correctness-Aware Self-Teacher Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")).
- •
  CAST is introduced: answer-free self-teacher scoring, asymmetric
  clipping, bidirectional advantage flipping, and a bounded
  zero-variance branch within the standard GRPO update.
- •
  Experiments on Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B show strong overall
  gains under a matched 300-step LoRA budget; appendix analyses report
  output length and generation-token budget sensitivity.

## 2 Preliminaries

Consider mathematical reasoning tasks with verifiable final
answers \[[3](#bib.bib21), [8](#bib.bib22), [14](#bib.bib28)\]. Given a
prompt $`x`$, a rollout/reference policy $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$
samples $`G`$ on-policy trajectories $`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$, where
$`y_{i}=(y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,T_{i}})`$. A verifier assigns a binary
reward $`r_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$ according to final-answer correctness. During
the subsequent policy update, $`\pi_{\theta}`$ denotes the online policy
being optimized and $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$ denotes the detached
policy used to sample the trajectories and compute reference
log-probabilities. Under answer-free self-teacher scoring, the
ground-truth answer is used only for verification.

GRPO \[[20](#bib.bib1)\] estimates a sequence-level advantage by
normalizing rewards within each sampled group:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\bar{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{std}}},\qquad\bar{r}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r_{j}.
``` |  | (1) |

The advantage is then assigned to all valid tokens and optimized with a
PPO-style clipped policy-gradient objective \[[19](#bib.bib20)\]. GRPO
is straightforward and verifier-grounded, but when all sampled
trajectories for a prompt are correct or all are incorrect, the reward
variance collapses and the normalized advantage becomes zero or
uninformative. These cases are denoted AllCorrect and AllWrong; groups
containing both outcomes are denoted Mixed.

CAST augments this sparse signal with a stop-gradient self-teacher. For
a teacher context $`c_{i}`$, define the token-level teacher–student gap

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{i,t}=\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid c_{i},y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}).
``` |  | (2) |

A token is *teacher-positive* when the teacher–student gap satisfies
$`g_{i,t}>0`$, meaning the self-teacher assigns higher log-probability
to the sampled token than the detached rollout/reference policy; it is
*teacher-negative* when $`g_{i,t}<0`$. Throughout this paper, the
“student” in teacher–student gap refers to this detached
rollout/reference policy $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$, rather than
the online policy after the current update begins. Prior self-distilled
RLVR methods usually use such gaps to modulate the magnitude of a
verifier-determined update, often without changing its sign. CAST
instead interprets the gap through trajectory-level correctness, because
teacher-positive tokens in incorrect trajectories and teacher-negative
tokens in correct trajectories should not be treated symmetrically.

In the default setting, CAST uses answer-free self-teacher scoring:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g^{\mathrm{AF}}_{i,t}=\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}).
``` |  | (3) |

Thus, the teacher observes only the prompt and generated prefix; the
ground-truth answer is reserved for the verifier. Additional background
on OPD/OPSD, DAPO-style GRPO variants, RLSD, and RLRT is given in
Appendix [8.1](#S8.SS1 "8.1 Related Work Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

All token-gap quantities used to construct CAST advantages are computed
on sampled tokens before the policy-gradient update and are treated as
detached coefficients inside the loss. Gradients therefore flow through
the policy-ratio term, not through the teacher–student gap or the
clipping operations used to build $`\tilde{A}_{i,t}`$.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Motivation: Correctness-Aware Self-Teacher Shaping

Self-distilled RLVR methods use On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) to
provide dense token-level guidance. Given a student rollout, OPSD
compares the probability assigned by a stop-gradient self-teacher and
the current student to each generated token. Standard OPSD treats this
teacher–student gap as a generic token preference: tokens with higher
teacher log-probability are encouraged, while tokens with lower teacher
log-probability are suppressed.

In RLVR, however, each trajectory is also labeled by verifier
correctness. This trajectory-level label changes how the teacher signal
should be interpreted. A teacher-positive token inside an incorrect
trajectory should not receive the same credit as one inside a correct
trajectory, and a correct trajectory may still contain locally
undesirable tokens such as redundant answer templates or termination
markers. Uniformly reinforcing every token in a successful rollout can
therefore consolidate spurious reasoning; conversely, local suppression
may benefit some teacher-negative tokens when the gap indicates low
support, while final advantage clipping limits over-suppression risk.

To make this concrete, an OPSD token-shift diagnostic on 2,048 rollouts
from 256 prompts (926 correct and 1,122 incorrect trajectories) compares
four strata formed by trajectory correctness and the sign of the
per-token gap
$`\Delta_{t}=\log p_{\mathrm{teacher}}(y_{t})-\log p_{\mathrm{student}}(y_{t})`$.
The diagnostic studies gap structure under an OPSD-style privileged
teacher context; all CAST training runs below use answer-free
self-teacher scoring
(Appendix [8.2](#S8.SS2 "8.2 Implementation Details for CAST Advantages ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")).
Appendix [8.3](#S8.SS3 "8.3 OPSD Token-Shift Diagnostic Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
defines the gap-weighted Top-$`K`$ stability metrics and reports
token-level interpretations.

| Stratum | Mean $`|\Delta|`$@10 | Var@10 | CV@10 $`\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{+}`$ | 0.433 | 2.038 | 4.133 |
| $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{-}`$ | 9.782 | 10.416 | 1.436 |
| $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{+}`$ | 0.509 | 2.506 | 3.841 |
| $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{-}`$ | 8.306 | 8.341 | 1.896 |

Table 1: Top-10 gap stability across correctness–sign strata in the OPSD
token-shift diagnostic ($`K{=}10`$). Lower CV@10 indicates more
repeatable gap mass on the dominant token types.

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Motivation: Correctness-Aware Self-Teacher Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
supports a correctness-aware reading of self-teacher gaps.
Teacher-negative tokens are much larger in magnitude than
teacher-positive tokens, so raw variance alone is scale-dominated; after
gap-weighted normalization, teacher-negative strata have the lowest
CV@10 and the most interpretable dominant tokens (e.g., termination and
answer-finalization markers). Teacher-positive tokens in incorrect
trajectories remain comparatively noisy. CAST therefore uses verifier
correctness to set trajectory-level direction, treats teacher-negative
tokens as a strong local suppression term, and allows only bounded
positive credit from teacher-positive tokens in incorrect trajectories
rather than trajectory-level imitation. Representative full-token maps
are given in
Appendix [8.9](#S8.SS9 "8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

### 3.2 Non-Privileged Self-Teacher Scoring

Under answer-free self-teacher scoring, CAST computes the self-teacher
gap for each token $`y_{i,t}`$ in trajectory $`y_{i}`$ as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{i,t}=\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`x`$ is the prompt, $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$ is the
detached rollout/reference student policy, and $`\pi_{\phi}`$ is a
stop-gradient self-teacher. The teacher receives the same problem
context and generated prefix as the student. The ground-truth answer and
reference solution are used only by the verifier to compute the binary
outcome reward, not in the self-teacher scoring context.
Reference-solution-conditioned teacher scoring is used only as an
ablation in
Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.3 Component Ablations ‣ 5 Ablation ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO");
implementation details are given in
Appendix [8.2](#S8.SS2 "8.2 Implementation Details for CAST Advantages ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

### 3.3 Trajectory-Level Base Advantage

For each prompt $`x`$, CAST samples $`G`$ on-policy trajectories
$`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ and obtains binary verifier rewards
$`r_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$. Let

|     |                                                                 |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \tau\in\{\textsc{Mixed},\textsc{AllCorrect},\textsc{AllWrong}\}
       ```                                                              |     |

denote the group type. In mixed groups, CAST uses the standard
group-relative GRPO advantage:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\bar{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\epsilon},\qquad\bar{r}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r_{j}.
``` |  | (5) |

When all sampled trajectories are correct or all are wrong, the reward
variance collapses and GRPO provides no useful group-relative signal.
CAST instead assigns a bounded correctness-aware base advantage:

|     |                                                         |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B_{i}=\begin{cases}A_{i},&\tau=\textsc{Mixed},\\
       +b_{\mathrm{correct}},&\tau=\textsc{AllCorrect},\\
       -b_{\mathrm{wrong}},&\tau=\textsc{AllWrong}.\end{cases}
       ```                                                      |     | (6) |

By default, $`b_{\mathrm{correct}}=b_{\mathrm{wrong}}=1`$. This branch
should be interpreted as a bounded verifier-signed shaping heuristic
rather than an unbiased group-relative advantage estimator. We choose
unit base values because final token advantages are clipped to
$`[-1.2,1.2]`$, which keeps the effective scale comparable to clipped
mixed-group updates.

This design prevents uniform-reward groups from receiving vanishing
updates. In standard GRPO, all-correct and all-wrong groups have
vanishing normalized advantages; in CAST, they still receive
sign-constrained base advantages and can therefore contribute bounded
token-level credit assignment. Consequently, CAST does not collapse to
standard GRPO solely because a rollout group has zero reward variance.

### 3.4 Correctness-Aware Token Weighting

CAST converts the teacher–student gap into a signed token weight:

|     |                                                             |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       z_{i,t}=\exp\left(\operatorname{sign}(B_{i})g_{i,t}\right).
       ```                                                          |     | (7) |

When $`B_{i}>0`$, a teacher-positive gap ($`g_{i,t}>0`$) means the
teacher assigns higher log-probability to the sampled token than the
student, so $`z_{i,t}>1`$ strengthens the positive update. When
$`B_{i}<0`$, the sign is reversed in this sign-preserving weighting
stage: a teacher-positive token in a negative-base trajectory receives
weaker negative pressure, while a teacher-negative token receives
stronger negative pressure. In our binary-reward mixed groups,
$`B_{i}=0`$ does not occur unless the group is uniform, and uniform
groups are handled separately by fixed-sign base advantages; for
completeness, a zero-base token can be masked or assigned zero
advantage. The next stage then allows sufficiently teacher-positive
negative-base tokens to undergo sign reversal into bounded positive
local credit.

CAST applies asymmetric clipping:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{clip}(z_{i,t},\ell_{+},u_{+}),&B_{i}>0,\\
\mathrm{clip}(z_{i,t},\ell_{-},u_{-}),&B_{i}<0.\end{cases}
``` |  | (8) |

By default,

|     |                                                                |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (\ell_{+},u_{+})=(0.8,1.05),\qquad(\ell_{-},u_{-})=(0.95,1.2).
       ```                                                             |     |

This biases shaping toward stronger teacher-negative suppression than
teacher-positive amplification: positive-base updates can be weakened
more than they can be amplified, and negative-base updates can be
strengthened more than they can be weakened. This reflects the empirical
observation that teacher-positive signals are often noisier, while
teacher-negative signals provide a more stable suppression term. The
incorrect-trajectory sign-reversal rule below reuses the smaller
positive cap $`u_{+}`$, so teacher-positive tokens inside negative-base
trajectories receive only bounded local positive credit.

### 3.5 CAST Token Advantage

CAST first forms a sign-preserving shaped advantage:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{A}_{i,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=B_{i}\left(1+\lambda(w_{i,t}-1)\right),`$ |  | (9) |

where $`\lambda`$ controls the strength of self-teacher shaping.

CAST then applies bidirectional local advantage sign reversal. For
positive-base trajectories, teacher-negative tokens can receive negative
token-level advantages. If $`B_{i}>0`$ and $`g_{i,t}<0`$, the teacher
assigns lower log-probability to the sampled token than the student.
CAST treats this as a local suppression term and forms a sign-reversed
candidate advantage:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A^{\mathrm{down}}_{i,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\lvert B_{i}\rvert\bigl(1+\lambda(w^{-}_{i,t}-1)\bigr),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle B_{i}>0,\ g_{i,t}<0,`$ |  | (10) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w^{-}_{i,t}=\mathrm{clip}\left(\exp(-g_{i,t}),\max(1,\ell_{-}),u_{-}\right).
``` |  | (11) |

For negative-base trajectories, teacher-positive tokens can receive
bounded positive token-level advantages. If $`B_{i}<0`$ and
$`g_{i,t}>0`$, CAST treats the token as locally useful partial reasoning
inside an otherwise incorrect trajectory and forms a sign-reversed
positive candidate advantage:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A^{\mathrm{up}}_{i,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\lvert B_{i}\rvert\bigl(1+\lambda(w^{+}_{i,t}-1)\bigr),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle B_{i}<0,\ g_{i,t}>0,`$ |  | (12) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w^{+}_{i,t}=\mathrm{clip}\left(\exp(g_{i,t}),\max(1,\ell_{+}),u_{+}\right).
``` |  | (13) |

The unclipped token advantage is then defined by the following case
distinction:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}A^{\mathrm{down}}_{i,t},&B_{i}>0\ \text{and}\ g_{i,t}<0,\\
A^{\mathrm{up}}_{i,t},&B_{i}<0\ \text{and}\ g_{i,t}>0,\\
\hat{A}_{i,t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (14) |

Finally, token advantages are clipped for numerical stability:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\tilde{A}_{i,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}\!\bigl(A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t},A_{\min},A_{\max}\bigr),`$ |  | (15) |

with default $`(A_{\min},A_{\max})=(-1.2,1.2)`$.

This token-level rule is the key difference between CAST and
correctness-unaware self-distillation. A correct trajectory is not
treated as uniformly positive at every token: locally teacher-negative
tokens can still be suppressed. Likewise, an incorrect trajectory is not
treated as uniformly negative at every token: locally teacher-positive
tokens can receive bounded positive credit, while the trajectory-level
verifier still determines the base sign and keeps the update grounded in
outcome correctness.

### 3.6 Optimization Objective

CAST uses the DAPO/GRPO clipped importance-ratio objective with
token-level advantages \[[19](#bib.bib20), [20](#bib.bib1),
[30](#bib.bib3)\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAST}}=-\mathbb{E}_{i,t}\left[\min\left(\rho_{i,t}\tilde{A}_{i,t},\mathrm{clip}\left(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right)\tilde{A}_{i,t}\right)\right],
``` |  | (16) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}.
``` |  | (17) |

The policy objective remains verifier-grounded at the trajectory level:
rewards determine trajectory correctness, group type, and the sign of
the base advantage. Answer-free self-teacher scoring then refines
token-level credit assignment through the gap $`g_{i,t}`$, and may
assign negative advantages to teacher-negative tokens within
positive-base trajectories or bounded positive advantages to
teacher-positive tokens within negative-base trajectories. The shaped
advantages are detached when optimizing this objective, so CAST does not
introduce gradients through the teacher-scoring computation.

Implementation details for the detached advantage construction are
provided in
Appendix [8.2](#S8.SS2 "8.2 Implementation Details for CAST Advantages ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

Method Token advantage Zero-variance groups Privileged information
Leakage risk GRPO / DAPO Sequence-level No No No OPSD Token-level No Yes
Yes GRPO+OPSD Sequence–token No Yes Yes RLSD / SDPO-style Token-level No

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Training Details

We train Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B \[[28](#bib.bib7)\] on
DAPO-Math-17K \[[30](#bib.bib3)\] for 300 optimizer steps under a
matched rollout and optimization budget. We verify no exact problem-text
overlap after normalization between DAPO-Math-17K and the in-domain
evaluation benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, MATH-500, and HMMT25).
The main comparison spans all three model sizes, while Qwen3-4B is used
for mechanistic ablations and diagnostics. All runs use
LoRA \[[9](#bib.bib6)\]. The RLVR-style methods use binary verifier
rewards, 8 completions per prompt, and 128 on-policy trajectories per
update; the OPSD-only baseline instead optimizes the
reference-solution-conditioned self-distillation objective.

All main runs fit on two NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs and use only a few
hundred optimizer steps. The comparison includes GRPO, OPSD, GRPO+OPSD,
RLSD, RLRT \[[12](#bib.bib17)\], and CAST. Here, OPSD denotes the
standard on-policy self-distillation objective without a
verifier-grounded GRPO term. The main method comparison uses a matched
300-step budget; 600-step CAST checkpoints are reported later only as
scaling evidence under longer training, not as the main matched-budget
comparison. GRPO+OPSD denotes an additive baseline,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO+OPSD}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\;+\;\alpha_{k}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}},
``` |  |

where $`\alpha_{k}`$ is the OPSD auxiliary coefficient. This baseline
does not use CAST’s correctness-aware group splitting, uniform-reward
base-advantage branch, answer-free self-teacher scoring, or
bidirectional advantage sign reversal. Full optimizer, decoding,
hardware, and method-specific hyperparameters are provided in
Appendix [8.4](#S8.SS4 "8.4 Training Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO");
additional training diagnostics are provided in
Appendix [8.5](#S8.SS5 "8.5 Training Diagnostics ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Training Details ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")

### 4.2 Results

For evaluation, each LoRA adapter is loaded on top of its corresponding
Qwen3 base model and evaluated with vLLM in the non-thinking generation
mode. Here, “non-thinking” means disabling the model-specific hidden
thinking mode; the model is still prompted to produce visible
step-by-step reasoning text. Following the multi-sample evaluation
practice common in mathematical reasoning \[[24](#bib.bib25),
[14](#bib.bib28)\], the protocol samples 16 responses per problem on
AIME24¹¹ 1
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime24](https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime24),
AIME25²² 2
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime25](https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime25),
AIME26³³ 3
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime26](https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime26),
MATH-500 \[[8](#bib.bib22)\]⁴⁴ 4
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500),
and HMMT25⁵⁵ 5
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/MathArena/hmmt_feb_2025](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MathArena/hmmt_feb_2025).
Pass@16 measures best-of-16 coverage, and Avg@16 measures average
per-sample accuracy. Full prompt, decoding, and verification details are
provided in
Appendix [8.6](#S8.SS6 "8.6 Evaluation Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
summarizes the main results across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B.
The exploratory RLSD variant that also updates all-correct and all-wrong
groups, denoted as RLSD (with zero-variance updates), is moved to
Appendix [8.8](#S8.SS8 "8.8 Additional Explorations ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
rather than included as a main baseline.

Across model scales, CAST improves Avg@16 and Pass@16 over the base
model. In the Qwen3-4B setting, CAST outperforms GRPO, OPSD, GRPO+OPSD,
RLSD, and RLRT on every benchmark under both metrics. The same matched
method set is evaluated on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B, where CAST gives the
strongest overall Avg@16 and competitive Pass@16, with the highest
Pass@16 in most comparisons. CAST also produces substantially longer
completions on average; length statistics and token-budget sweeps are
reported in Appendix
Tables [13](#S8.T13 "Table 13 ‣ 8.6 Evaluation Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
and [14](#S8.T14 "Table 14 ‣ 8.6 Evaluation Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").
Its gains are strongest under sufficiently large generation budgets,
while under tight token budgets the advantage can shrink or disappear.

CAST shifts probability mass away from the all-failure (0/16) stratum
and toward medium-to-high success strata. Relative to the base model,
all-failure problems decrease from 16 to 7 on AIME24, from 15 to 9 on
AIME26, and from 23 to 15 on HMMT25, while the combined 5–15/16 and
16/16 strata increase from 7 to 16, from 6 to 16, and from 4 to 7,
respectively.

## 5 Ablation

### 5.1 Self-Teacher Shaping Cutoff

CAST uses answer-free self-teacher scoring. This ablation varies when
the CAST-specific token shaping is removed. For cutoff step $`K`$, the
token-gap coefficient is kept constant before $`K`$ and set to zero
afterward:

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \lambda_{k}^{\mathrm{cutoff}}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{0},&k<K,\\
       0,&k\geq K.\end{cases}
       ```                                                             |     | (18) |

For this cutoff ablation, the uniform-reward base branch is also gated
after step $`K`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b^{\mathrm{cutoff}}_{\mathrm{correct},k}=b^{\mathrm{cutoff}}_{\mathrm{wrong},k}=\begin{cases}1,&k<K,\\
0,&k\geq K.\end{cases}
``` |  | (19) |

This schedule imposes a hard cutoff. The ablation tests whether CAST
benefits from persistent correctness-aware token shaping. Once
$`k\geq K`$, teacher–student gaps no longer affect token-level
advantages, and the uniform-reward base advantages are also disabled.
Thus, after the cutoff, all-correct and all-wrong groups no longer
receive CAST-specific fixed base-advantage updates. With zero-based
optimizer indices $`k=0,\ldots,299`$ over 300 updates, the cutoff-at-300
setting ($`K=300`$) keeps both teacher-gap shaping and uniform-reward
base-advantage updates active for every update.

Table 7: Component ablations for CAST in the Qwen3-4B, 300-step setting.
The first row is the default CAST configuration; subsequent rows ablate
one component at a time. All rows report Avg@16 and Pass@16 under the
same evaluation protocol.

#### 5.3.1 Zero-Variance Group Updates

The *Mixed-only* variant keeps CAST’s answer-free self-teacher gap,
asymmetric clipping, and bidirectional sign reversal on mixed groups,
but disables the all-correct/all-wrong uniform-reward branch. Thus,
Mixed-only versus CAST tests whether zero-variance groups add useful
signal beyond mixed-group token shaping.

#### 5.3.2 Teacher Scoring Context

The default CAST configuration uses answer-free self-teacher scoring
(Appendix [8.2](#S8.SS2 "8.2 Implementation Details for CAST Advantages ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")).
The *With ground-truth answer* ablation instead conditions the teacher
on the dataset reference solution $`y^{\ast}`$ (the verified
final-answer string from training metadata, identical to the verifier’s
ground truth) before scoring the on-policy rollout:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{\mathrm{GT}}(x,y^{\ast})=\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace x\lx@text@rbrace}\;\|\;\texttt{"\textbackslash n\textbackslash n[Reference solution]\textbackslash n"}\;\|\;\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace solution\lx@text@rbrace\textbackslash n\textbackslash n[Student response]\textbackslash n"},
``` |  |

where solution is set to $`y^{\ast}`$, $`\|`$ denotes string
concatenation, and, at token $`y_{i,t}`$, the teacher is evaluated on
the prefix $`T_{\mathrm{GT}}(x,y^{\ast})\|y_{i,<t}`$. This matches the
privileged reference-solution teacher template used in OPSD-style
training, while keeping CAST’s correctness-aware token shaping and
zero-variance branch. The ablation tests whether answer-free
self-teacher scoring is necessary or whether this privileged context
provides comparable token-level guidance.

#### 5.3.3 Token-Weight Clipping

The two symmetric-clipping rows replace CAST’s asymmetric token-weight
ranges with symmetric alternatives. This ablation tests whether the
proposed positive- and negative-base clipping asymmetry contributes
beyond using a bounded teacher-gap weight.

#### 5.3.4 Bidirectional Advantage Sign Reversal

The *No sign reversal* variant keeps the uniform-reward branch,
answer-free self-teacher scoring, and asymmetric clipping, but prevents
local sign changes in both directions. Thus, teacher-negative
positive-base tokens cannot become negative, and teacher-positive
negative-base tokens cannot become positive. This ablation isolates the
role of two-sided local correction beyond sign-preserving token-gap
weighting.

## 6 Limitations

Several limitations remain.

- •
  Scale. The experiments evaluate Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
  with LoRA and up to 600 optimizer steps. Larger models, longer
  training, full-parameter updates, and broader model families remain
  untested.
- •
  Diagnostic scope. Mechanistic analyses are limited primarily to the
  300-step Qwen3-4B setting and an OPSD diagnostic set. Broader
  answer-free self-teacher-gap diagnostics would further test the
  mechanism.
- •
  Non-thinking evaluation. CAST is trained and evaluated with extended
  reasoning disabled. Explicit chain-of-thought generation is left to
  future work.
- •
  Efficiency and sensitivity. CAST uses validation-tuned clipping and
  token-gap hyperparameters, and it often produces longer outputs. This
  may improve exploration but also increases inference cost; length- or
  compute-normalized evaluation would be useful.

## 7 Conclusion

This work introduced CAST (Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric
Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO). CAST combines
verifier-grounded trajectory correctness with answer-free self-teacher
scoring, allowing token-level advantages to depend on both rollout
correctness and teacher–student gaps. This design can suppress locally
teacher-negative tokens in correct rollouts and provide bounded positive
credit to locally teacher-positive tokens in incorrect rollouts,
requires no reference reasoning traces, and does not expose the
ground-truth answer or reference solution to the self-teacher.

Under a matched rollout and optimization budget, CAST achieves the
strongest overall Avg@16 in the comparisons and improves Pass@16 over
GRPO, OPSD, GRPO+OPSD, RLSD, and RLRT on mathematical reasoning
benchmarks. The results suggest that correctness-aware token shaping can
make self-distilled RLVR more reliable, especially when zero-variance
groups are explicitly used rather than discarded.

## 8 Appendix

1: Online policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, rollout/reference policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$, stop-gradient self-teacher
$`\pi_{\phi}`$, verifier $`\mathcal{V}`$, prompts $`\mathcal{D}`$, group
size $`G`$

2: Shaping coefficient $`\lambda`$, base advantages
$`b_{\mathrm{correct}},b_{\mathrm{wrong}}`$

3: Weight clips $`(\ell_{+},u_{+})`$ and $`(\ell_{-},u_{-})`$,
token-advantage clip range $`(A_{\min},A_{\max})`$

4: for each training step $`k`$ do

5:   Set rollout/reference policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\leftarrow\mathrm{sg}(\pi_{\theta})`$

6:   Sample prompts $`\{x_{b}\}\sim\mathcal{D}`$

7:   for each prompt $`x_{b}`$ do

8:    Sample rollouts
$`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x_{b})`$

9:    Compute verifier rewards $`r_{i}=\mathcal{V}(x_{b},y_{i})`$

10:    Classify group type
$`\tau_{b}\in\{\textsc{Mixed},\textsc{AllCorrect},\textsc{AllWrong}\}`$

11:    if $`\tau_{b}=\textsc{Mixed}`$ then

12:      Compute GRPO advantages $`A_{i}`$

13:    end if

14:    for each trajectory $`y_{i}`$ do

15:      Set base advantage

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B_{i}\leftarrow\begin{cases}A_{i},&\tau_{b}=\textsc{Mixed},\\
       +b_{\mathrm{correct}},&\tau_{b}=\textsc{AllCorrect},\\
       -b_{\mathrm{wrong}},&\tau_{b}=\textsc{AllWrong}.\end{cases}
       ```                                                            |     |

16:      for each valid token $`y_{i,t}`$ do

17:       Compute answer-free self-teacher gap

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{sg}\Big(\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid x_{b},y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x_{b},y_{i,<t})\Big)
``` |  |

18:       $`z_{i,t}\leftarrow\exp(\operatorname{sign}(B_{i})g_{i,t})`$

19:       if $`B_{i}>0`$ then

20:         $`w_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(z_{i,t},\ell_{+},u_{+})`$

21:       else

22:         $`w_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(z_{i,t},\ell_{-},u_{-})`$

23:       end if

24:       if $`B_{i}>0`$ and $`g_{i,t}<0`$ then

25:
        $`w^{-}_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(\exp(-g_{i,t}),\max(1,\ell_{-}),u_{-})`$

26:
        $`A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}\leftarrow-\lvert B_{i}\rvert\bigl(1+\lambda(w^{-}_{i,t}-1)\bigr)`$

27:       else if $`B_{i}<0`$ and $`g_{i,t}>0`$ then

28:
        $`w^{+}_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(\exp(g_{i,t}),\max(1,\ell_{+}),u_{+})`$

29:
        $`A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}\leftarrow\lvert B_{i}\rvert\bigl(1+\lambda(w^{+}_{i,t}-1)\bigr)`$

30:       else

31:
        $`A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t}\leftarrow B_{i}\left(1+\lambda(w_{i,t}-1)\right)`$

32:       end if

33:
      $`\tilde{A}_{i,t}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}\!\bigl(A^{\mathrm{raw}}_{i,t},A_{\min},A_{\max}\bigr)`$

34:      end for

35:    end for

36:   end for

37:   Update $`\pi_{\theta}`$ using the clipped DAPO/GRPO objective with
$`\tilde{A}_{i,t}`$

38:   Periodically refresh the stop-gradient self-teacher
$`\pi_{\phi}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta}`$

39: end for

Algorithm 1 CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with
Advantage Flipping for GRPO

### 8.1 Related Work Details

##### DAPO-style GRPO variants.

Recent GRPO variants improve training stability for long-horizon
reasoning. DAPO \[[30](#bib.bib3)\], for example, introduces asymmetric
clipping, dynamic sampling, token-level policy-gradient loss, and
overlong reward shaping. The experiments adopt its asymmetric clipping
rule,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}),\qquad\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}>\epsilon,
``` |  | (20) |

which gives positive-advantage tokens a larger upper clipping range.
DAPO handles zero-variance groups mainly through dynamic sampling,
whereas CAST gives such groups bounded sign-constrained base advantages.

##### Zero-variance prompt handling in GRPO.

All-correct and all-wrong groups are commonly handled before the policy
update rather than inside the advantage estimator. A standard
preprocessing strategy is to discard or resample groups whose sampled
rewards have zero variance, because their group-normalized GRPO
advantages are zero. DAPO’s dynamic sampling follows this philosophy: it
seeks to build updates from prompts whose sampled completions contain
both correct and incorrect responses, thereby concentrating computation
on prompts that provide relative ranking signal \[[30](#bib.bib3)\].
This is effective for gradient utilization, but it also changes the
on-policy prompt distribution toward boundary-difficulty examples and
leaves no direct learning signal from prompts that are currently too
easy or too hard.

Recent work argues that zero-variance prompts should not necessarily be
discarded. RL-ZVP/No Prompt Left Behind keeps all-correct and all-wrong
prompts and constructs entropy-guided advantages so that easy prompts
can still consolidate confident behavior and hard prompts can still
receive exploratory pressure \[[13](#bib.bib14)\].
ERPO \[[16](#bib.bib18)\] similarly focuses on residual prompts whose
sampled outcomes lack informative reward contrast, using an
entropy-aware policy objective and adaptive sampling to reactivate these
cases. Prompt Replay addresses a related sampling problem by maintaining
an online prompt buffer and replaying prompts that are likely to produce
informative, non-saturated rollouts \[[2](#bib.bib19)\]. These methods
operate mainly at the prompt-selection or auxiliary-shaping level. CAST
is complementary: it keeps zero-variance groups in the same GRPO-style
update, assigns only bounded verifier-signed base advantages, and uses
the answer-free self-teacher gap to decide which tokens within those
all-correct or all-wrong trajectories should be amplified or suppressed.

##### OPD and OPSD.

On-Policy Distillation (OPD) uses an external teacher to provide
token-level supervision on student-sampled trajectories, reducing
off-policy mismatch between teacher-generated data and student-visited
states. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) removes the external teacher
by using a stop-gradient self-teacher, often with privileged contexts
such as the ground-truth answer or verified solution
traces \[[32](#bib.bib4)\]. Although OPSD supplies dense token
information, its direction is teacher-driven rather than
verifier-grounded. Prior work suggests that OPSD may be more reliable
for compacting successful reasoning than repairing failed
trajectories \[[11](#bib.bib2)\], motivating correctness-aware use of
self-teacher signals.

##### Reasoning self-improvement and self-training.

CAST is also related to methods that improve reasoning from
model-generated traces. Chain-of-thought prompting and self-consistency
show that intermediate reasoning paths and multiple sampled solutions
can substantially improve mathematical and symbolic
reasoning \[[26](#bib.bib24), [24](#bib.bib25)\]. STaR bootstraps
reasoning by fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that lead to
correct answers \[[31](#bib.bib26)\], while ReST generates policy
samples and reuses filtered data for reinforced
self-training \[[6](#bib.bib27)\]. CAST differs from these offline or
prompt-time self-improvement approaches by shaping on-policy RLVR
updates directly, using verifier correctness to decide the
trajectory-level direction and an answer-free self-teacher gap to refine
token-level credit assignment.

##### Self-distilled RLVR.

Self-distilled RLVR methods such as RLSD, SDPO-style training, and
related hidden-distillation variants seek to combine two complementary
signals: the verifier reward decides whether a rollout should be
encouraged or discouraged, while the teacher-student gap provides dense
token-level structure inside the rollout \[[29](#bib.bib5),
[10](#bib.bib13), [5](#bib.bib16)\]. This design is attractive because
it keeps the update anchored to outcome correctness while avoiding the
extreme sparsity of sequence-level rewards. It also explains why
RLSD-type baselines are stronger than OPSD-only training in these
experiments: they do not merely imitate the teacher, but use the
verifier to set the rollout-level direction.

Most RLSD-style objectives, however, use the teacher–student gap
primarily as a magnitude modulator rather than as a source of signed
token-level feedback. A typical formulation maps the gap to a bounded
weight,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{i,t}=\mathrm{clip}\left(\exp(\mathrm{sign}(A_{i})g_{i,t}),1-\delta,1+\delta\right),
``` |  | (21) |

and sets

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \tilde{A}_{i,t}=A_{i}\left((1-\lambda)+\lambda w_{i,t}\right).
       ```                                                             |     | (22) |

This preserves the GRPO update sign through $`A_{i}`$ while using
distillation for dense token shaping. Consequently, every token in a
positive-advantage trajectory remains positive and every token in a
negative-advantage trajectory remains negative; the teacher gap changes
the strength, but not the local direction, of the update. This is a
conservative and stable choice, but it is limited when a correct
trajectory contains locally undesirable tokens or when an incorrect
trajectory contains locally useful partial reasoning.

Another limitation is data utilization. Since the base sign is inherited
from the group-relative advantage, all-correct and all-wrong groups
become weak or receive zero group-relative advantage when $`A_{i}=0`$.
These groups are common in RLVR training: easy prompts may become
all-correct, while hard prompts may remain all-wrong. Discarding or
ignoring them wastes verifier-labeled trajectories that could still
teach consolidation or failure avoidance. Finally, some
self-distillation setups score the teacher with the ground-truth answer
or a reference solution in the context, creating a privileged
token-scoring signal that is stronger than what the policy would have at
inference time.

CAST keeps the useful verifier anchoring of RLSD-style training but
changes all three design choices. First, it interprets teacher gaps
through trajectory correctness and allows two-sided local sign changes:
teacher-negative tokens inside correct trajectories can receive negative
token-level advantages, and teacher-positive tokens inside incorrect
trajectories can receive bounded positive token-level advantages.
Second, it gives all-correct and all-wrong groups bounded
sign-constrained base advantages, so zero-variance data remains active.
Third, it uses answer-free self-teacher scoring and reserves
ground-truth answers and reference solutions for verification only.

##### RLRT and advantage sign reversal.

RLRT provides a different interpretation of the teacher–student
gap \[[12](#bib.bib17)\]. Instead of treating teacher-negative tokens as
uniformly undesirable, it reverses the teacher signal on
verified-correct trajectories so that tokens where the student departs
from the teacher can be strengthened. This is motivated by the
observation that a smaller or lagged teacher may suppress alternative
valid reasoning paths that the student has discovered. RLRT is therefore
closely related to the advantage sign-reversal motivation in CAST: both
methods reject pure teacher imitation on successful rollouts. CAST
differs in three ways. It uses answer-free self-teacher scoring, applies
the gap asymmetrically according to both trajectory correctness and gap
sign with bidirectional local sign reversal, and explicitly uses
uniform-reward all-correct and all-wrong groups through bounded base
advantages.

### 8.2 Implementation Details for CAST Advantages

CAST constructs token-level advantages in two separated stages. First,
after rollouts and verification, teacher and student log-probabilities
are computed on the sampled tokens to form a detached gap

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{g}_{i,t}=\mathrm{sg}\left[\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})\right],
``` |  | (23) |

where $`\theta_{\mathrm{old}}`$ denotes the student parameters used for
rollout/log-probability collection before the policy-gradient update.
This detached $`\bar{g}_{i,t}`$, together with the detached verifier
reward, is used to build $`\tilde{A}_{i,t}`$. Second, the online policy
is updated only through the importance ratio $`\rho_{i,t}`$ in the
DAPO/GRPO objective. Thus, gradients are not propagated through the
teacher logits, the old-policy student logits used in the gap, the
exponentiation, or the clipping operations that define the shaped
advantages.

For mixed groups, $`B_{i}`$ is the usual group-normalized GRPO
advantage. For AllCorrect and AllWrong groups, $`B_{i}`$ is set to
$`+b_{\mathrm{correct}}`$ and $`-b_{\mathrm{wrong}}`$, respectively.
These fixed base-advantage values determine only the sign and bounded
scale of the token-level update; they do not create a separate reward
model and do not expose the answer to the self-teacher. Truncated
completions are masked out before advantage construction, so
uniform-reward base-advantage updates are applied only to valid
generated tokens.

### 8.3 OPSD Token-Shift Diagnostic Details

##### Diagnostic setup.

The token-shift study samples 256 prompts from DAPO-Math-17K with 8
on-policy completions per prompt (2,048 trajectories total), using the
base Qwen3-4B model under the same non-thinking generation settings as
the main experiments. Verifier labels split the rollouts into 926
correct and 1,122 incorrect trajectories. For gap analysis only, the
teacher is scored with an OPSD-style privileged context that includes
the reference solution; this isolates the structure of teacher–student
gaps and is distinct from the answer-free self-teacher scoring used by
CAST at training time.

##### Strata.

For each generated token, define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{t}=\log p_{\mathrm{teacher}}(y_{t})-\log p_{\mathrm{student}}(y_{t}).
``` |  |

Teacher-positive tokens have $`\Delta_{t}>0`$ and teacher-negative
tokens have $`\Delta_{t}<0`$. Combining trajectory correctness with gap
sign yields four strata:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{B}\in\{\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{+},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{-},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{+},\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{-}\}.
``` |  |

##### Gap-weighted Top-$`K`$ stability.

Rather than comparing only token counts, the analysis studies the
stability of token types that dominate gap mass in each stratum. For
vocabulary type $`v`$, aggregate gap weight is

|     |                                                                 |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       M_{\mathcal{B},v}=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B},\;y_{t}=v}|\Delta_{t}|.
       ```                                                              |     |

Tokens are ranked by $`M_{\mathcal{B},v}`$. For token $`v`$, define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu_{\mathcal{B},v}=\mathbb{E}\left[|\Delta_{t}|\mid t\in\mathcal{B},\;y_{t}=v\right],\qquad\sigma^{2}_{\mathcal{B},v}=\mathrm{Var}\left[|\Delta_{t}|\mid t\in\mathcal{B},\;y_{t}=v\right].
``` |  |

The gap-weighted raw variance is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Var@K}(\mathcal{B})=\frac{\sum_{v\in\mathrm{TopK}(\mathcal{B})}M_{\mathcal{B},v}\sigma^{2}_{\mathcal{B},v}}{\sum_{v\in\mathrm{TopK}(\mathcal{B})}M_{\mathcal{B},v}},
``` |  |

and the gap-weighted coefficient of variation is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{CV@K}(\mathcal{B})=\frac{\sum_{v\in\mathrm{TopK}(\mathcal{B})}M_{\mathcal{B},v}\sigma_{\mathcal{B},v}/\mu_{\mathcal{B},v}}{\sum_{v\in\mathrm{TopK}(\mathcal{B})}M_{\mathcal{B},v}}.
``` |  |

Lower $`\mathrm{CV@K}`$ indicates that the dominant token types in a
stratum receive gap mass more repeatably. Raw variance is
scale-sensitive: a token with consistently large $`|\Delta_{t}|`$ can
have high variance even when its relative variation is low.

##### Findings and token interpretations.

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Motivation: Correctness-Aware Self-Teacher Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
in the main text reports $`K{=}10`$ statistics. Two patterns motivate
CAST. First, teacher-negative signals have much larger absolute
magnitude than teacher-positive signals: the top-10 mean $`|\Delta|`$ is
$`9.782`$ in $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{-}`$ versus $`0.433`$ in
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{+}`$, and $`8.306`$ in
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{-}`$ versus $`0.509`$ in
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{+}`$. This scale difference explains why
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{-}`$ and
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{-}`$ also have larger raw Var@10.

Second, after gap-weighted normalization, teacher-negative strata are
more stable. $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{corr}}^{-}`$ has the lowest CV@10
($`1.436`$), and $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{-}`$ remains much lower
than $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{+}`$ ($`1.896`$ versus $`3.841`$).
The dominant teacher-negative tokens are high-magnitude but relatively
stable types such as \<\|im_end\|\>, Answer, whitespace, and repeated
format markers. In contrast, $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{inc}}^{+}`$ is
dominated by locally plausible symbolic tokens such as +, \\, \$,
whitespace, parentheses, and digits, indicating that teacher-positive
mass in incorrect trajectories is comparatively diffuse and less
suitable as uniform positive supervision.

### 8.4 Training Details

Unless otherwise specified, experiments use DAPO-Math-17K for 300
optimizer steps on Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B. DAPO-Math-17K is
used only for training; we verify no exact problem-text overlap after
normalization with the evaluation benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AIME26,
MATH-500, and HMMT25), so reported results are not affected by
exact-match train–test contamination. The main method comparison applies
the same protocol and matched baseline set across all three model sizes,
while mechanistic ablations and diagnostics use Qwen3-4B. The
training-step ablation additionally evaluates CAST checkpoints at 100
and 600 steps for each model size. LoRA with rank 64 and alpha 128 is
used while keeping the backbone frozen. LoRA adapters are applied to
q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj. Each
run uses two NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs: one for vLLM rollouts and one for
policy optimization. For each prompt, 8 on-policy completions are
sampled. With prompt batch size 2 and gradient accumulation 8, each
optimizer update contains 16 prompt groups and 128 trajectories. This
resource-constrained configuration uses a rollout micro-batch of 2
prompts, and the default run stops after 300 optimizer steps rather than
relying on long-horizon or large-cluster post-training.

Training uses bfloat16 precision, scaled dot-product attention (SDPA),
gradient checkpointing, maximum prompt length 1024, and maximum
completion length 3072. Unless otherwise specified, generation uses
temperature 0.7, top-$`p`$ 0.95, top-$`k`$ 20, min-$`p`$ 0.0, repetition
penalty 1.0, and presence penalty 0.2. Completions that reach the
maximum completion length without termination are masked from the policy
loss, so uniform-reward base-advantage updates apply only to valid,
non-truncated completion tokens. The optimizer is AdamW with zero weight
decay. The learning rate is $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ with 5% warmup and
polynomial decay to $`1\times 10^{-7}`$, and the maximum gradient norm
is 1.0. Rewards are binary verifier correctness rewards; no additional
format or repetition rewards are used. Following DAPO, all GRPO-style
methods use asymmetric clipping with $`\epsilon=0.2`$ and
$`\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28`$, and set the Kullback-Leibler (KL)
coefficient to 0.

For self-distillation methods, the stop-gradient teacher is refreshed
every 10 optimizer steps unless a baseline uses a fixed teacher. OPSD
uses the reference-solution-conditioned OPSD objective with coefficient
1.0 and no verifier-grounded GRPO term. GRPO+OPSD adds the standard OPSD
token auxiliary to the GRPO objective, using an auxiliary coefficient
initialized to 0.2 and linearly decayed over 50 steps; it does not use
CAST’s correctness-aware group handling or advantage sign reversal. RLSD
uses verifier rewards to set rollout-level directions and
teacher–student gaps to modulate token-level magnitudes, with
token-level weights clipped to $`[0.8,1.2]`$. RLRT follows the
reversed-teacher rule on verified-correct
trajectories \[[12](#bib.bib17)\]: it forms
$`d_{i,t}=\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})-\log\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,t}\mid c_{i},y_{i,<t})`$,
clips $`w_{i,t}=\exp(\mathrm{sign}(A_{i})d_{i,t})`$ to
$`[1-\epsilon_{w},1+\epsilon_{w}]`$ with $`\epsilon_{w}=1.0`$, and sets
$`\tilde{A}_{i,t}=A_{i}[(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{RLRT}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{RLRT}}w_{i,t}]`$
with $`\lambda_{\mathrm{RLRT}}=0.5`$ and no decay. This reweighting is
applied only to verified-correct rollouts; incorrect rollouts retain the
standard GRPO sequence advantage. The RLRT teacher context uses the
problem plus a successful rollout sampled for the same prompt group when
available. CAST uses a token-gap coefficient of 1.0 with no decay and
answer-free self-teacher scoring:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{\mathrm{AF}}(x)=\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace x\lx@text@rbrace}\;\|\;\texttt{"\textbackslash n\textbackslash n[Student response]\textbackslash n"},
``` |  |

so the teacher context excludes the ground-truth answer and reference
solution. The *With ground-truth answer* ablation in
Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.3 Component Ablations ‣ 5 Ablation ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
instead uses

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{\mathrm{GT}}(x,y^{\ast})=\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace x\lx@text@rbrace}\;\|\;\texttt{"\textbackslash n\textbackslash n[Reference solution]\textbackslash n"}\;\|\;\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace solution\lx@text@rbrace\textbackslash n\textbackslash n[Student response]\textbackslash n"},
``` |  |

with solution set to $`y^{\ast}`$ from reward_model.ground_truth on
DAPO-Math-17K. In both settings, the verifier alone uses the ground
truth to compute binary correctness rewards.

GRPO uses only verifier rewards and group-relative advantages. OPSD uses
token-level self-distillation on on-policy rollouts without verifier
rewards. GRPO+OPSD combines the GRPO policy-gradient loss with standard
OPSD token distillation, but its OPSD signal remains correctness-unaware
and does not reactivate zero-variance groups. RLSD combines GRPO with
OPSD-style token weighting by using verifier rewards to determine
rollout-level update directions and teacher–student gaps to modulate
token-level magnitudes. RLRT further emphasizes exploration by treating
teacher-negative tokens in correct rollouts as potentially useful
departures from the teacher. CAST uses the same GRPO training loop, but
interprets teacher–student gaps according to trajectory correctness. In
the main CAST configuration, token shaping is applied to mixed,
all-correct, and all-wrong groups; zero-variance groups receive bounded
sign-constrained base advantages instead of being dropped. CAST uses
asymmetric token-weight clipping with $`(\ell_{+},u_{+})=(0.8,1.05)`$
for positive-base trajectories and $`(\ell_{-},u_{-})=(0.95,1.2)`$ for
negative-base trajectories, applies negative sign reversal to
teacher-negative positive-base tokens and bounded positive sign reversal
to teacher-positive negative-base tokens under the smaller positive-base
cap, and clips final token-level advantages to $`[-1.2,1.2]`$.

In terms of training cost, CAST requires about $`1.25\times`$ the
wall-clock time of GRPO for a full 300-step run. A full CAST run takes
about 5 hours, compared with about 4 hours for GRPO, 4 hours and 40
minutes for RLSD, and 4 hours and 30 minutes for OPSD. The extra cost is
modest and mainly comes from computing self-teacher logits for token-gap
shaping and applying correctness-aware token-level advantages. See
Table [8](#S8.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 8.4 Training Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

advantage sign reversal are handled, training diagnostics from the main
Qwen3-4B CAST run are also summarized. Values in
Table [9](#S8.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 8.5 Training Diagnostics ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
are means over 300 optimizer steps. The run contains a nontrivial
fraction of zero-variance prompt groups: all-correct groups account for
20.2% of prompt groups and all-wrong groups for 31.3%, while mixed
groups account for 48.5%. Thus, the uniform-reward branch is not an
isolated edge case under this training setup.

late-stage entropy decrease under correctness-unaware self-distillation,
while GRPO often assigns zero group-relative advantage to many rollout

contrast and motivating CAST’s bounded zero-variance branch.

### 8.6 Evaluation Details

All methods are evaluated under a common vLLM-based protocol. The base
model is evaluated directly; trained methods use the LoRA checkpoint
from optimizer step 300 unless an ablation explicitly studies a
different checkpoint step. Evaluation is conducted on held-out
benchmarks—AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, MATH-500, and HMMT25—for which we
found no exact normalized problem-text overlap with DAPO-Math-17K,
reducing exact-match train–test contamination risk. For each problem, 16
completions are sampled, and Pass@$`k`$ is reported with
$`k\in\{1,4,8,16\}`$. Answers are extracted from the final \boxed{}
expression and verified for mathematical equivalence with math_verify
when available. See
Table [10](#S8.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 8.6 Evaluation Details ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO").

All evaluation datasets are free-form mathematical reasoning benchmarks,
so a single boxed-answer prompt is used:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | {problem}\n\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}. |  |

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Configuration | Value |
| Model sizes | Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B |
| Ablation/diagnostic setting | Qwen3-4B |
| Evaluated checkpoint | LoRA checkpoint at step 300 unless otherwise specified |
| Evaluation datasets | AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, MATH-500, HMMT25 |
| Train–test overlap | No exact overlap after normalized problem-text matching |
| Evaluation backend | vLLM |
| Hardware | 2 $`\times`$ NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs |
| Tensor parallel size | 2 |
| Precision | bfloat16 |
| Attention backend | FlashAttention |
| Max model length | 40960 |
| Max new tokens | 32768 |
| Hidden thinking mode | Disabled; visible step-by-step reasoning prompted |
| Tokenizer / chat template | Base-model tokenizer forced |
| Samples per problem | 16 |
| Reported metrics | Pass@1, Pass@4, Pass@8, Pass@16 |
| Temperature | 0.7 |
| Top-$`p`$ / Top-$`k`$ / Min-$`p`$ | 0.8 / 20 / 0.0 |
| Presence penalty | 0.0 |
| Seed | 42 |
| GPU memory utilization | 0.9 |
| Generation batch size | 16 for AIME/HMMT; 64 for MATH-500 |
| Number of evaluated examples | All examples in each benchmark |
| Answer format | Final answer in \boxed{} |
| Answer verification | math_verify with boxed-answer fallback |

#### 8.8.1 RLSD

The RLSD baseline applies token-level shaping on top of the
sequence-level GRPO advantage. It improves over sparse sequence-level
feedback by using the teacher–student token log-probability gap to
modulate each token’s advantage. However, this formulation still depends
on the original group-relative advantage, which becomes weak when all
sampled responses for a prompt are correct or all are incorrect.

#### 8.8.2 RLSD with Zero-Variance Updates

The RLSD (zero-variance updates) variant additionally applies RLSD-style
updates to all-correct and all-wrong groups. Because this changes the
handling of zero-variance groups while retaining the RLSD shaping rule,
it is treated as an exploratory variant rather than as the main RLSD
baseline.

#### 8.8.3 Strict RLSD

Strict RLSD addresses this issue by splitting groups into mixed,
all-correct, and all-wrong cases. Mixed groups keep the original GRPO
advantage, while all-correct and all-wrong groups receive explicit fixed
base advantages. This gives nonzero training signal even when
group-relative normalization would otherwise collapse.

#### 8.8.4 Flip RLSD

This variant introduces local advantage sign reversal. A token from a
positive-advantage rollout can still receive negative credit if the
teacher–student gap is negative. This avoids uniformly reinforcing every
token in a globally successful response and makes the token-level
feedback more selective.

#### 8.8.5 Flip RLSD without Ground-Truth Teacher Reference

This variant switches to answer-free self-teacher scoring by removing
the reference solution from the teacher prompt, so the token-level
signal depends only on the problem and the student response. This
variant tests whether RLSD can provide useful token-level supervision
without access to the ground-truth solution or reference solution.

#### 8.8.6 Flip RLSD without Ground-Truth Reference and without Decay

This variant keeps the token-gap shaping active throughout training
instead of annealing it away. It treats the teacher–student token gap as
a persistent training signal rather than only as an early-stage
regularizer.

#### 8.8.7 CAST with Incorrect-Path Positive Flipping

CAST adds the final bidirectional sign-reversal rule: teacher-negative
positive-base tokens receive negative reversal, and teacher-positive
negative-base tokens receive bounded positive reversal under the
positive-base clipping cap. This is the configuration used in the main
results.

### 8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals

To make the token-level motivation concrete,
Figures [5](#S8.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Correct rollout. ‣ 8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
and [6](#S8.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Incorrect rollout. ‣ 8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
visualize every token in two representative OPSD diagnostic
trajectories. The diagnostic setup uses an OPSD-style teacher context
with a reference answer; these figures illustrate teacher–student gap
behavior only and do not depict answer-free self-teacher scoring as used
by CAST at training time. For each generated token $`y_{t}`$, define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{t}=\log\pi_{\mathrm{teacher}}(y_{t}\mid\mathrm{context},y_{<t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{student}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).
``` |  |

Green tokens have $`\Delta_{t}>0`$ (teacher-positive); red tokens have
$`\Delta_{t}<0`$ (teacher-negative). Darker colors indicate larger
$`|\Delta_{t}|`$. Blank colored cells correspond to whitespace tokens,
and \n marks newline tokens.

##### Correct rollout.

Figure [5](#S8.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Correct rollout. ‣ 8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
shows a compact but complete correct rollout with 537 generated tokens.
The reference answer is 13, and the generated answer is “Answer:
13\<\|im_end\|\>”, so the trajectory receives verifier reward 1.0. In
this trajectory, 306 tokens are teacher-positive, 215 are
teacher-negative, and 16 are nearly unchanged; the total
teacher-positive weight is 53.89, while the total teacher-negative
weight is 104.96. Thus, even a correct rollout contains many local
tokens that the teacher would down-weight rather than reinforce.

signals for one correct trajectory. The rollout reaches the correct
answer, but teacher-negative tokens appear throughout the reasoning

supports the CAST design choice of allowing token-level credit
correction inside globally correct rollouts rather than assigning
uniformly positive advantages to every token.

##### Incorrect rollout.

Figure [6](#S8.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Incorrect rollout. ‣ 8.9 Full-Trajectory Token Map of Teacher-Positive and Teacher-Negative Signals ‣ 8 Appendix ‣ CAST: Non-Privileged Clipped Asymmetric Self-Teaching with Advantage Flipping for GRPO")
shows a complementary incorrect trajectory: the reference answer is
2040, while the generated answer is “120”. It contains 561 generated
tokens, with 291 teacher-positive tokens, 256 teacher-negative tokens,
and 14 nearly unchanged tokens. The teacher-positive weight is 45.67,
while the teacher-negative weight is 85.75. Even an incorrect rollout
can contain many locally teacher-positive tokens, so teacher-positive
signals alone should not be treated as positive supervision without
verifier-grounded trajectory direction.

Figure 6: Full-token map of teacher-positive and teacher-negative
signals for one incorrect trajectory. Although the final answer is
wrong, many intermediate mathematical and structural tokens are still
teacher-positive. This supports the CAST choice to interpret
teacher–student gaps through verifier-grounded trajectory correctness
rather than using token-level self-distillation as correctness-unaware
imitation.

### 8.10 Complete MATH-500 Trajectory Example

This section includes a compact qualitative example from the Qwen3-4B
MATH-500 evaluation outputs.We select one group of trajectories from
MATH-500 because the first sampled completions from the base model and
the GRPO checkpoint are both verified as incorrect, while the first
sampled CAST completion is verified as correct. The three trajectories
use the same change-of-base and telescoping idea, so the comparison
isolates a small but decisive cancellation error. The raw
Markdown-formatted generations are re-typeset below as response cards,
with decorative separators removed.

##### Problem.

Find the value of

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log_{2}{3}\cdot\log_{3}{4}\cdot\log_{4}{5}\cdot\log_{5}{6}\cdot\log_{6}{7}\cdot\log_{7}{8}.
``` |  |

The ground-truth answer is $`3`$.
````
